title: Reinvestigating the Uncovered Interest Rate Parity Puzzle via Analysis of Multivariate Tail Dependence in Currency Carry Trades

extraction.methodology_summary: The paper investigates the risk-reward profile of currency carry trades by analyzing the multivariate tail dependence of currency baskets. Currencies are sorted daily into five baskets based on their interest rate differentials (forward-to-spot ratio) relative to the US dollar, focusing on the high interest rate (long) and low interest rate (short) baskets. The joint distribution of exchange rate log-returns is modeled using a two-stage Inference Function for the Margins (IFM) approach, combining Log-Generalized-Gamma marginal distributions with flexible mixture copula models (Clayton-Frank-Gumbel). Finally, the authors compute generalized multivariate tail dependence coefficients to evaluate downside and upside extreme risk exposures and adjust cumulative portfolio returns.

key_findings: The Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP) condition is violated empirically, allowing investors to earn profits on average via the currency carry trade.

High interest rate (investment) currencies exhibit significant upper tail dependence during crisis periods, meaning they tend to depreciate simultaneously against the USD, exposing carry trade portfolios to severe drawdown risks.
Low interest rate (funding) currencies and high interest rate currencies display periods of inverted tail dependence, which may reflect the construction phase of carry trade positions by investors.
Incorporating multivariate tail dependence into risk-reward analysis reveals that the apparent profitability of carry trades is a compensation for exposure to joint catastrophic tail risk.

The Clayton-Frank-Gumbel (C-F-G) mixture copula model provides a superior fit compared to the Clayton-Gumbel (C-G) and outer-power Clayton (OpC) models for capturing asymmetric tail dependence in currency baskets.
limitations: The analysis does not quantify a market price per unit of tail risk (referred to as relative exposure adjustments only).

The study removes euro area countries (due to ERM convergence trade) and several pegged currencies (HKD, KWD, MYR, SAR, and Danish krone) which might limit the generalizability to all global currencies.
The model assumes local stationarity over sliding windows of 6 months and 1 year.
The VIX is used as a proxy for market volatility, but it is not a direct measure of global FX volatility.
